docs.title: Cloudmesh AI llm-mock (Mock LLM Provider)
docs.text: cloudmesh-ai-llm-mock is a professional-grade, OpenAI-compatible mock LLM service designed for developers and testers. It allows you to simulate various LLM providers and production-grade failures without needing actual GPU infrastructure or expensive API keys, making it the perfect tool for CI/CD pipelines, local development, and resilience testing.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• OpenAI-Compatible API: Implements the standard /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, and /v1/embeddings endpoints. Swap real LLM endpoints for this mock server with zero code changes.
  • Multi-Provider Simulation: High-fidelity simulation of different providers (Ollama, vLLM, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock), including provider-specific response headers and error formats (Quirks).

  • Chaos Engineering Engine: Test your application's resilience by simulating real-world API instability:

    • Random Failures: Inject 429 (Rate Limit) and 500 (Internal Error) responses.
    • Simulated Latency: Configure min/max delays to test timeout handling.
    • TPM & Context Limits: Simulate Tokens-Per-Minute limits and Context Window overflows.
    • GPU OOM Simulation: Restrict which models are "loaded" to simulate memory errors.
    • The Meltdown Profile: A one-click catastrophic failure sequence (Latency $\rightarrow$ Total Failure $\rightarrow$ Service Unavailable).
    • Scenario-Based Mocking: Move beyond static strings. Use keyword-based templates to simulate specific behaviors like Safety Refusals, Hallucinations, or Edge-Case Responses.

    • Dual-Interface GUI:

    • User Chat UI (/chat): A polished, real-time markdown chat interface with a live latency monitor.

    • Admin Dashboard (/admin): A powerful control center to toggle chaos settings, manage loaded models, and edit scenarios in real-time.
    • Observability Mocks: Includes mock /health and /metrics endpoints to test Kubernetes probes and monitoring stacks.

docs.title: 1. Installation
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/cloudmesh-ai/cloudmesh-ai-llm-mock.git
cd cloudmesh-ai-llm-mock
pip install -e .

docs.title: 2. Using the Mock Server
docs.text:
Start the server to expose the OpenAI-compatible API:

cmm serve --port 8888

The server is now available at http://localhost:8888.

Explore the Interfaces:

  • User Chat UI: http://localhost:8888/chat
  • Admin Dashboard: http://localhost:8888/admin
  • API Documentation: http://localhost:8888/docs

Example API call:

curl http://localhost:8888/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "ollama-llama3",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
  }'

docs.title: 3. Using the CLI
docs.text:
The cmm command allows you to interact with the mock providers directly:

# Send a prompt using the default provider
cmm prompt "What is Cloudmesh AI?"

# Switch the active provider to vLLM
cmm provider set vllm

# List available models for the active provider
cmm list

docs.title: Mock Provider Matrix
docs.text: Provider Simulated Behavior Key Models Implementation Ollama Local-first LLM feel llama3, mistral, phi3 ✅ Mocked vLLM High-throughput API feel gpt-4-mock, mixtral ✅ Mocked Anthropic Claude-style responses & headers claude-3-opus, haiku ✅ Mocked Azure OpenAI Enterprise API feel & quirks gpt-4, gpt-35-turbo ✅ Mocked AWS Bedrock AWS-style error formats titan, claude-v2 ✅ Mocked

docs.title: Docker Deployment
docs.text:
Run the mock server using Docker for an isolated setup:

# Start the server in the background
docker-compose up -d

The server will be available at http://localhost:8888. Your configuration is persisted via a volume mount to ~/.config/cloudmesh/ on your host machine.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The project ensures consistency across mock providers using a tiered testing strategy:

  • Unit Tests: Verify that each provider returns the expected mock format.
  • API Tests: Validate the FastAPI routes against the OpenAI API specification.
  • Compliance Suite: Ensures all mock providers implement the same base interface.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: We welcome contributions to add new mock providers or expand the simulated API responses. Please see Contributing for guidelines.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text: Cloudmesh AI llm-mock is designed as a Mock Service, providing a thin, OpenAI-compatible layer over a set of simulated LLM providers. It focuses on simulating not just the "happy path" of an AI response, but the complex, often unpredictable nature of production LLM APIs.

docs.title: 1. Mock API Server (FastAPI)
docs.text: The server implements the standard OpenAI REST API. It acts as the entry point for external applications. - Request Validation: Uses Pydantic to ensure incoming requests match the OpenAI specification. - Routing: Maps API endpoints (like /v1/chat/completions) to the internal provider logic. - Dynamic Dispatch: Routes requests to different BaseProvider implementations based on the model parameter in the request. - Quirk Formatting: Before returning a response or error, the server applies a Provider Quirk Profile to ensure the response headers and error bodies match the real-world provider being simulated.

docs.title: 2. The Chaos Engine
docs.text: Located within the server state, the Chaos Engine intercepts requests to simulate real-world instability: - Failure Injection: Randomly injects 429 (Too Many Requests) or 500 (Internal Server Error) responses based on a configurable failure rate. - Latency Simulation: Adds a random delay within a specified range to test client-side timeouts and loading states. - TPM & Context Enforcement: Tracks "Tokens Per Minute" (TPM) and maximum context window size, returning 429 or 400 errors when limits are exceeded. - GPU OOM Simulation: Maintains a set of "Loaded Models." If a request specifies a model not in this set, the server returns a 404, simulating an Out-of-Memory error on the provider side. - Meltdown Mode: A catastrophic failure sequence that progresses through three stages: Max Latency $\rightarrow$ 100% Failure $\rightarrow$ Service Unavailable (503).

docs.title: 3. Scenario Manager
docs.text: To provide high-fidelity responses, cmm uses a keyword-based scenario system: - Scenario Templates: Predefined response patterns (e.g., "Safety Refusal", "Hallucination"). - Keyword Matching: The manager scans the user prompt for specific keywords. If a match is found, the corresponding scenario template is used instead of the generic response. - Runtime Management: Scenarios can be created, edited, or deleted via the Admin GUI and are persisted to ~/.config/cloudmesh/scenarios.json.

docs.title: 4. Provider Abstraction Layer
docs.text: To simulate different LLM behaviors, the project uses a provider pattern: - BaseProvider: An abstract base class defining the required interface (prompt, list_models, tokenize). - Concrete Providers: Specific implementations (e.g., OllamaProvider, AnthropicProvider) that define their own model lists and quirk profiles.

docs.title: 5. Control Interfaces
docs.text:
• CLI Orchestrator: A cmm command for server management, quick prompting, and provider configuration.
  • User Chat UI: A polished frontend for interacting with the mock LLM and visualizing latency.
  • Admin Dashboard: A real-time control panel for the Chaos Engine and Scenario Manager.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
External Request $\rightarrow$ FastAPI Route $\rightarrow$ Chaos Engine Check $\rightarrow$ Provider Factory $\rightarrow$ Scenario Matcher $\rightarrow$ Deterministic Mock Response $\rightarrow$ Quirk Profile Formatting $\rightarrow$ OpenAI-Formatted JSON

graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[FastAPI]
    B --> C[Chaos Engine]
    C --> D[Provider]
    D --> E[Scenario Matcher]
    E --> F[Response]

docs.title: Chaos Engineering Guide
docs.text:
The Chaos Engine in Cloudmesh AI llm-mock is designed to help you build resilient LLM applications. In the real world, LLM APIs are not perfectly stable—they experience latency spikes, rate limits, and occasional catastrophic failures.

By simulating these conditions, you can ensure your application handles errors gracefully, implements proper retry logic, and provides a good user experience even when the backend is struggling.

docs.title: Chaos Features
docs.text: You can configure all chaos settings in real-time via the Admin Dashboard (/admin).

docs.title: 1. Random Failures
docs.text: Simulate intermittent API instability by setting a Failure Rate. - How it works: For every request, the server rolls a die. If the result is within the failure rate, the request fails. - Simulated Errors: The server randomly injects either a 429 Too Many Requests or a 500 Internal Server Error. - Use Case: Test if your application implements exponential backoff and retry logic.

docs.title: 2. Simulated Latency
docs.text: Test how your UI handles slow responses by configuring a Latency Range (Min/Max). - How it works: The server adds a random delay between the minimum and maximum configured values before returning the response. - Use Case: Verify that your frontend displays loading states and that your API clients have appropriate timeout settings.

docs.title: 3. The Meltdown Profile
docs.text:
The Panic Button in the Admin Dashboard triggers "Meltdown Mode," a simulated cascading service failure that progresses through three stages:

Stage Duration Effect Simulated State 1. Degradation 0-15s Max Latency The API becomes extremely slow. 2. Outage 15-30s 100% Failure Every request returns a 500 Internal Server Error. 3. Collapse 30s+ Service Unavailable The API returns 503 Service Unavailable.

Use Case: Test how your system behaves during a total provider outage and whether your failover mechanisms (e.g., switching to a backup provider) trigger correctly.

docs.title: 4. TPM (Tokens Per Minute) Limiting
docs.text: Simulate the strict rate limits imposed by providers like OpenAI or Anthropic. - How it works: The server tracks the number of tokens processed per minute. If the limit is exceeded, it returns a 429 Too Many Requests error with a Retry-After header. - Use Case: Test your token-counting logic and rate-limiting middleware.

docs.title: 5. Context Window Simulation
docs.text: Test how your application handles prompts that are too large for the model. - How it works: You can configure a maximum Context Window (in tokens). If the prompt (or the combined prompt and response) exceeds this limit, the server returns a 400 Bad Request. - Use Case: Verify that your application correctly truncates history or warns the user when the context limit is reached.

docs.title: 6. GPU OOM (Out-of-Memory) Simulation
docs.text: Simulate the behavior of a provider that can only load a limited number of models into VRAM. - How it works: In the Admin Dashboard, you can specify a list of Loaded Models. If a request is made for a model not in this list, the server returns a 404 Not Found, simulating an OOM error or a model-not-loaded state. - Use Case: Test your application's ability to handle "Model Not Found" errors and prompt the user to select a different model.

docs.title: Testing Recipes
docs.text: Transform the Chaos Engine's features into solutions for specific production problems. Use these recipes to validate your application's resilience.

docs.title: Recipe: The "Flaky API"
docs.text:
Goal: Test exponential backoff and retry logic.

Configuration Steps: 1. Open the Admin Dashboard (/admin). 2. Set the Failure Rate to 5%. 3. Set the Latency Range to Min: 1s, Max: 3s.

What to look for: - Ensure the application does not immediately surface an error to the user on the first failure. - Verify that retries occur with increasing delays (exponential backoff). - The request should eventually succeed once the random failure roll passes.

docs.title: Recipe: The "Cold Start"
docs.text:
Goal: Test handling of model loading/OOM errors.

Configuration Steps: 1. Open the Admin Dashboard (/admin). 2. Locate the Loaded Models list. 3. Remove the model your application is currently targeting from the list.

What to look for: - The server will return a 404 Not Found (simulating a GPU OOM or unloaded model). - Verify that the application handles this gracefully (e.g., by notifying the user that the model is loading or automatically falling back to a different available model).

docs.title: Recipe: The "Safety Wall"
docs.text:
Goal: Test if the application correctly handles safety refusals without crashing.

Configuration Steps: 1. Send a prompt containing restricted keywords such as "illegal" or "exploit". 2. Ensure the server is configured to return a standard safety refusal for these terms.

What to look for: - The application should receive the refusal response from the API. - The UI should display the refusal message clearly to the user. - Verify that no unhandled exceptions or "empty response" errors are triggered in the frontend.

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text: The Cloudmesh AI llm-mock tool is accessed via the cmm command. It serves as a developer's interface to manage and test mock LLM providers.

docs.title: Command Summary
docs.text: Command Description cmm serve Start the OpenAI-compatible mock API server cmm init Initialize the default configuration file cmm prompt "<text>" Send a prompt to the active mock provider cmm list List available models for the active provider cmm provider set <name> Set the active mock provider (e.g., ollama, vllm) cmm provider get Show the current active mock provider

docs.title: Starting the Mock Server
docs.text:
# Start the server on default port 8888
cmm serve

# Start the server on a custom port
cmm serve --port 9000

docs.title: Prompting and Provider Management
docs.text:
# Prompt the default mock provider
cmm prompt "Hello, mock LLM!"

# Switch to the vLLM mock provider
cmm provider set vllm

# List all available mock models for vLLM
cmm list

# Override provider for a single prompt
cmm prompt "Test this!" --provider ollama

docs.title: Configuration Guide
docs.text: Cloudmesh AI llm-mock uses a combination of a static YAML configuration file for defaults and a dynamic runtime state managed via the Admin GUI.

docs.title: Static Configuration
docs.text: Configuration is stored in ~/.config/cloudmesh/llms-mock.yaml. This file determines the default behavior when the server starts.

docs.title: Environment Variable Overrides
docs.text: You can override any configuration setting using environment variables. This is particularly useful for Docker deployments or CI/CD pipelines where you don't want to manage a physical YAML file.

docs.title: Naming Convention
docs.text:
Environment variables must start with the CMM_ prefix, followed by the configuration path in uppercase. For nested settings, use underscores (_) as separators.

Target Setting Environment Variable Example Value active_provider CMM_ACTIVE_PROVIDER vllm providers.ollama.default_model CMM_PROVIDERS_OLLAMA_DEFAULT_MODEL llama2 providers.vllm.default_model CMM_PROVIDERS_VLLM_DEFAULT_MODEL gpt-4-mock

docs.title: Smart Type Casting
docs.text: The system automatically casts environment variable values to the correct data type based on the existing value in the YAML file: - Booleans: true/false (case-insensitive) - Numbers: Automatically detected as int or float - Strings: Default fallback

docs.title: Dynamic Keys
docs.text:
If you provide an environment variable for a key that doesn't exist in the YAML file, the system will automatically create that key in the configuration object for the current session.

Usage Example:

# Override the active provider and a nested model setting
export CMM_ACTIVE_PROVIDER=vllm
export CMM_PROVIDERS_VLLM_DEFAULT_MODEL=mixtral-8x7b

cmm serve

Environment variables take absolute precedence over the settings in the YAML file.

docs.title: Configuration Schema
docs.text:
# The provider used by the 'cmm prompt' command by default
active_provider: "ollama"

# Provider-specific settings
providers:
  ollama:
    default_model: "llama3"
  vllm:
    default_model: "gpt-4-mock"
  anthropic:
    default_model: "claude-3-sonnet"
  azure:
    default_model: "gpt-4"
  bedrock:
    default_model: "anthropic.claude-v2"

docs.title: Managing Configuration via CLI
docs.text:
You can modify the active provider without editing the file manually:

# Set the active provider to vllm
cmm provider set vllm

# Verify the current setting
cmm provider get

docs.title: Runtime Configuration (Admin GUI)
docs.text:
While the YAML file sets the defaults, the Admin Dashboard (/admin) allows you to change critical server behaviors in real-time without restarting the server.

Setting Description Effect Active Provider The provider used for requests that don't specify a model. Changes the response style and headers. Failure Rate % of requests that fail randomly. Triggers 429 or 500 errors. Latency Range Min/Max delay in seconds. Simulates slow network/inference. TPM Limit Max tokens processed per minute. Triggers 429 errors when exceeded. Context Window Max tokens for prompt + response. Triggers 400 errors when exceeded. Loaded Models List of models currently "in VRAM". Triggers 404 errors for missing models.

docs.title: Scenario Configuration
docs.text:
Scenarios are persisted in ~/.config/cloudmesh/scenarios.json. While these are best managed via the Admin GUI, you can edit the JSON file directly for bulk updates.

Format:

{
    "scenario_id": [
        ["keyword1", "keyword2"], 
        "Response template text"
    ]
}

docs.title: Server Startup Configuration
docs.text: The mock server (cmm serve) can be configured via CLI flags: - --host: Specify the network interface (default: 127.0.0.1). - --port: Specify the listening port (default: 8888). - --kill-port: Kill any process using the port before starting (default: true).

docs.title: Contributing Guide
docs.text: We welcome contributions to make Cloudmesh AI llm-mock a better tool for LLM developers!

docs.title: Adding a New Mock Provider
docs.text:
To simulate a new LLM provider (e.g., a mock for a new cloud offering), follow these steps:

  1. Create the Provider Class: Create a new file in cmm/providers/ (e.g., new_provider.py) that inherits from BaseProvider.
  2. Implement Required Methods:
    • prompt(): Return a mock response that mimics the style of the provider.
    • list_models(): Return a list of models that the real provider would offer.
    • get_name(): Return a unique identifier for the provider.
  3. Define Provider Quirks:
    • Open cmm/quirks.py.
    • Create a new ProviderQuirkProfile that defines the specific error format and default headers for your provider.
    • Register the profile in the QUIRK_PROFILES dictionary.
    • In your provider class, implement get_quirk_profile_name() to return the key you used in QUIRK_PROFILES.
  4. Register the Provider: Add your new provider class to the _PROVIDERS dictionary in cmm/providers/__init__.py.
  5. Update Documentation: Add the new provider to the Mock Provider Matrix in README.md.

docs.title: Improving Mock Realism
docs.text: We encourage contributors to make the mock responses more realistic. Instead of simple strings, consider: - Using Scenario Templates: Add new default scenarios to scenarios.py to handle specific user intents. - Adding Random Delays: Implement custom get_model_speed() logic in your provider to simulate different model sizes. - Implementing Simulated Error Codes: Ensure your ProviderQuirkProfile maps HTTP status codes (429, 500, etc.) to the provider's authentic error codes.

docs.title: Testing Your Changes
docs.text:
Ensure your changes don't break existing mocks:

# Run unit tests for providers
PYTHONPATH=. pytest tests/unit

docs.title: Pull Request Process
docs.text:
1. Create a feature branch.
  2. Ensure all tests pass.
  3. Submit a PR with a clear description of the mock behavior you've added or improved.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text: To transform the Cloudmesh AI llm-mock server into a full simulation environment, we are implementing two distinct graphical user interfaces (GUIs): an Admin GUI for server management and a User GUI for simulating the end-user chat experience.

docs.title: 2. Technology Stack (The "Lean Stack")
docs.text:
To maintain the project's portability and avoid a complex frontend build pipeline, we use the following open-source tools:

  • Backend: FastAPI (Python)
  • Templating: Jinja2 (Server-side HTML rendering)
  • Reactivity: HTMX (Client-side dynamic updates via HTML attributes)
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS (via CDN for modern, responsive design)
  • Communication: Standard JSON and Server-Sent Events (SSE) for streaming

docs.title: 3.1 Admin GUI (/admin)
docs.text:
The Admin GUI is the "control room" for the mock server.

Key Features: - Provider Management: A dropdown to change the active_provider globally. - Chaos Engine Controls: - Failure Rate: A slider to set the percentage of requests that should return errors (429, 500). - Latency Simulation: A slider to set the artificial response delay (min/max). - Scenario Toggles: Checkboxes to enable/disable specific scenarios (e.g., "Safety Refusals"). - Model State: A list of available models with toggles to simulate "Loaded" vs "Unloaded" states. - Real-time Monitor: A log stream showing incoming requests, the triggered provider, and the scenario used.

docs.title: 3.2 User GUI (/chat)
docs.text:
The User GUI simulates a real-world LLM chat application.

Key Features: - Chat Window: A modern, scrollable conversation history. - Model Selector: A dropdown to choose the target model (calling /v1/models). - Streaming Output: Real-time token-by-token rendering using the server's SSE implementation. - Markdown Rendering: Integrated marked.js for rich text, tables, and Prism.js for syntax highlighting in code blocks. - Latency Visualization: A real-time latency meter in the header that tracks inter-token arrival times during streaming. - Session Management: 'Clear Chat' functionality to reset the local conversation history. - Settings: Simple toggles for "Stream" mode and "Temperature".

docs.title: 4.1 Route Mapping
docs.text: Route Method Description /admin GET Renders the Admin Dashboard. /admin/config POST Updates server settings (Provider, Chaos, Latency). /admin/logs GET Returns the latest server logs as HTML fragments. /chat GET Renders the Chat Interface. /chat/send POST Handles user message and returns the initial response. /chat/stream GET SSE endpoint for streaming the model response.

docs.title: 4.2 State Management
docs.text:
Since the server is a singleton, a global ServerState object will be implemented in base_server.py to track: - active_provider: Current default provider. - failure_rate: Probability of simulated error. - latency_range: Tuple of (min_delay, max_delay). - loaded_models: Set of models currently "active" in memory.

The BaseLLMProvider and base_server routes will consult this ServerState before processing every request.

docs.title: Getting Started: Your First 15 Minutes with Cloudmesh AI llm-mock
docs.text:
Welcome to Cloudmesh AI llm-mock! This interactive tutorial is designed to get you up and running in minutes. Instead of just showing you how to start the server, we're going to walk you through a complete "resilience loop": from a successful request to a total system meltdown, and finally, how to fix your code to handle it.

By the end of this guide, you'll understand how to use cmm to battle-test your LLM application.

docs.title: 1. Install cmm
docs.text:
First, ensure you have Python 3.10+ installed. If you've cloned the repository, install the package in editable mode:

git clone https://github.com/cloudmesh-ai/cloudmesh-ai-llm-mock.git
cd cloudmesh-ai-llm-mock
pip install -e .

docs.title: 2. Start the Server
docs.text:
Launch the mock server to expose the OpenAI-compatible API:

cmm serve

The server is now running at http://localhost:8888. Keep this terminal open!

docs.title: 3. Send a Successful Prompt
docs.text: Let's verify everything is working. You can do this in two ways:

docs.title: Option A: Using the User GUI (Recommended)
docs.text: Open your browser and go to: http://localhost:8888/chat Type a message and hit enter. You should see a smooth, streaming response.

docs.title: Option B: Using curl
docs.text:
Open a new terminal and run:

curl http://localhost:8888/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "ollama-llama3",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello! Are you working?"}]
  }'

Result: You should receive a JSON response with a successful AI completion.

docs.title: 4. Trigger a "Meltdown"
docs.text:
Now for the fun part. Real-world APIs don't always work. Let's simulate a catastrophic provider failure using the Admin Dashboard.

  1. Open your browser to: http://localhost:8888/admin
  2. Scroll down to the Panic Button section.
  3. Click the "Trigger Meltdown" button.

You have just activated Meltdown Mode.

docs.title: 5. Observe the Failure
docs.text:
The Meltdown Profile doesn't just crash the server; it simulates a cascading failure. Try sending another prompt via the Chat UI or curl and watch what happens over the next 30 seconds:

Time What you'll see What's happening 0-15s Extreme slowness Degradation: The server injects maximum latency. Your app might hang or time out. 15-30s 500 Internal Server Error Outage: Every single request now fails immediately. 30s+ 503 Service Unavailable Collapse: The service is completely offline.

Notice: If your application crashed or showed a raw error message to the user, you've found a resilience gap!

docs.title: 6. Fix the Application
docs.text:
How do we stop a provider "meltdown" from breaking our user experience? The gold standard is implementing Exponential Backoff and Retries.

Instead of a simple API call, wrap your request in a retry loop. Here is a conceptual example using Python and the popular tenacity library:

import requests
from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential, retry_if_exception_type

# We only want to retry on server errors (500, 503) or rate limits (429)
def is_retryable_error(exception):
    if isinstance(exception, requests.exceptions.HTTPError):
        return exception.response.status_code in [429, 500, 503]
    return False

@retry(
    stop=stop_after_attempt(5), 
    wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=1, min=2, max=10),
    retry=retry_if_exception_type(requests.exceptions.HTTPError)
)
def call_llm_with_retry(prompt):
    response = requests.post(
        "http://localhost:8888/v1/chat/completions",
        json={"model": "ollama-llama3", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()

try:
    print(call_llm_with_retry("Hello!"))
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Even after retries, the service is down: {e}")

docs.title: Why this helps:
docs.text:
1. Wait Exponential: Instead of hammering the server, it waits 2s, then 4s, then 8s... giving the provider time to recover.
  2. Graceful Failure: By catching the final exception, you can show the user a friendly message ("Our AI is taking a nap, please try again in a moment") instead of a crash.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
You've mastered the basics! Now that you know how to trigger a meltdown, explore the other Chaos tools in the Admin Dashboard: - Failure Rate: Inject random 429s to test your retry logic more subtly. - TPM Limits: Test how your app handles strict token quotas. - GPU OOM: Simulate "Model Not Found" errors by restricting the Loaded Models list.

Happy testing!

docs.title: GUI Guide
docs.text: Cloudmesh AI llm-mock provides two distinct web interfaces to make interacting with and managing the mock server intuitive and efficient.

docs.title: 1. User Chat Interface (/chat)
docs.text: The User Chat Interface is designed to simulate the end-user experience of an LLM application. It allows you to test prompts and visualize the performance of the mock providers.

docs.title: Key Features:
docs.text:
• Real-Time Interaction: Send messages to the active mock provider and receive streaming responses.
  • Markdown Rendering: Full support for markdown, including formatted code blocks and tables, ensuring that you see exactly how the final AI response will be rendered.
  • Live Latency Monitor: A built-in monitor that visualizes the simulated server delay for every response, making it easy to see the effect of Chaos Engine latency settings.
  • Provider Integration: The chat interface automatically fetches available models from the /v1/models endpoint, allowing you to switch models on the fly.

Access it at: http://localhost:8888/chat

docs.title: 2. Admin Dashboard (/admin)
docs.text: The Admin Dashboard is the "control room" for your mock environment. It allows you to change the server's behavior in real-time without restarting the process.

docs.title: A. Server Configuration
docs.text: Directly modify the global state of the mock server: - Active Provider: Switch the default provider (e.g., from ollama to azure). - Failure Rate: Set the percentage of requests that should fail with 429 or 500 errors. - Latency Range: Set the min/max delay (in seconds) for responses. - TPM Limit: Configure the Tokens-Per-Minute limit to test rate-limiting. - Context Window: Set the maximum token limit to test prompt truncation. - Loaded Models: Enter a comma-separated list of models that are "in VRAM." Any model not on this list will trigger a 404 GPU OOM simulation.

docs.title: B. Scenario Manager
docs.text: Manage the keyword-based response system: - Create/Edit/Delete: Add new scenarios or modify existing ones to simulate safety refusals, hallucinations, or specific edge cases. - Instant Updates: Changes made in the dashboard are saved to scenarios.json and applied to the next request immediately.

docs.title: C. The Panic Button
docs.text: Toggles Meltdown Mode, which simulates a cascading service failure (Latency $\rightarrow$ Outage $\rightarrow$ Collapse). Use this to test your system's absolute worst-case scenario.

docs.title: D. Live Server Logs
docs.text:
A real-time stream of server events. Chaos events (like triggered failures or latency injections) are highlighted in red, allowing you to correlate API errors with the Chaos Engine's actions.

Access it at: http://localhost:8888/admin

docs.title: Installation Guide
docs.text:
This guide describes how to install and run the Cloudmesh AI llm-mock service.

!!! note "System Requirements" Cloudmesh AI llm-mock requires Python 3.10 or newer. If you are using a version manager like pyenv or conda, ensure your active environment meets this requirement.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer
  • Pip (Python package installer)

docs.title: From Source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/cloudmesh-ai/cloudmesh-ai-llm-mock.git
cd cloudmesh-ai-llm-mock
pip install -e .

docs.title: Running the Mock Server
docs.text:
The mock server provides an OpenAI-compatible API. To start it:

cmm serve

Once started, the server will be available at http://localhost:8888.

docs.title: Local LLM Setup (Ollama)
docs.text: To use the "Real" mode with local models (like Phi-3), you need to install Ollama:

docs.title: 1. Install Ollama
docs.text:
• macOS: Download and install the app from ollama.com.
  • Linux: Run the official installation script: bash curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
  • Windows: Download and run the installer from ollama.com.

docs.title: 2. Pull the Model
docs.text:
After installing and starting Ollama, pull the Phi-3 model:

ollama pull phi3

docs.title: 3. Enable Real Mode and Verify
docs.text: You can enable "Real" mode through the Admin Dashboard: 1. Navigate to http://localhost:8888/admin. 2. Expand the Real LLM Service section. 3. Click "Run All" to verify the Ollama engine, model availability, inference, and latency. 4. Once the check is complete, the real model (e.g., ollama-phi3-real) will automatically become available in the chat interface.

docs.title: Testing the Server
docs.text:
You can test the server using curl:

curl http://localhost:8888/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "ollama-llama3",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
  }'

docs.title: Interactive API Docs
docs.text:
FastAPI automatically generates interactive documentation. Visit: http://localhost:8888/docs

Next Steps: Now that you have the server running, learn how to Configure the Mock Providers to match your target environment.

docs.title: Comprehensive Scenario Library
docs.text: Static mock responses (like "I am a helpful AI") are often insufficient for testing real-world edge cases. Cloudmesh AI llm-mock uses a Scenario-Based Mocking system that allows you to simulate specific model behaviors based on the content of the user's prompt.

docs.title: How Scenarios Work
docs.text:
A scenario consists of a set of Keywords and a Response Template.

When a request arrives, the Scenario Manager scans the prompt for any of the configured keywords. If a match is found, the manager returns the corresponding template instead of the generic fallback response.

docs.title: The Matching Process:
docs.text:
1. Input Analysis: The prompt is converted to lowercase.
  2. Keyword Search: The system iterates through all active scenarios.
  3. Template Selection: The first scenario that has a keyword present in the prompt is selected.
  4. Fallback: If no keywords match, the generic_helpful scenario is used as the final fallback.

docs.title: Managing Scenarios
docs.text: Scenarios are managed in real-time via the Admin Dashboard (/admin).

docs.title: Creating and Editing Scenarios
docs.text: In the Admin Dashboard, you can: - Add a New Scenario: Provide a unique ID, a comma-separated list of keywords, and the response text. - Edit Existing Scenarios: Modify keywords or templates for an existing scenario. - Delete Scenarios: Remove outdated scenarios (except the generic_helpful fallback).

docs.title: Scenario Persistence
docs.text:
All scenarios are persisted in a JSON file located at ~/.config/cloudmesh/scenarios.json. You can edit this file manually if you prefer to bulk-import scenarios.

Example scenarios.json format:

{
    "safety_refusal": [
        ["hack", "password", "illegal"],
        "I'm sorry, but I cannot assist with this request as it violates safety policies."
    ],
    "hallucination": [
        ["fact", "calculate"],
        "Actually, the moon is made of lunar-cheese, according to recent 2027 studies."
    ]
}

docs.title: Recommended Scenarios for Testing
docs.text:
To get the most out of cmm, we recommend creating the following types of scenarios:

Scenario Type Keywords Purpose Safety/Policy illegal, exploit, bypass Test how your app displays refusals to the user. Hallucinations fact, who is, when did Test how your app handles confidently wrong information. Edge Cases weird, strange, complex Test if your UI breaks with unusually formatted responses. Integration Triggers trigger_action, book_flight Test if your application's function-calling or agentic logic triggers correctly.

docs.title: Standard Test Scenarios
docs.text: This library provides a set of pre-defined scenarios designed to stress-test your application's resilience, UI, and processing logic.

docs.title: Edge Cases
docs.text:
These scenarios test how your application handles unexpected or extreme data formats.

Scenario ID Suggested Keywords Example Response Template Testing Goal edge_long_response long_response, overflow This is an extremely long response designed to test UI boundaries. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit. Sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua. [Repeated 100x] Test UI overflow, word-wrapping, and scrolling behavior. edge_empty_response empty_response, null_test (Empty String) Test null handling, empty state messages, and app stability. edge_invalid_json invalid_json, parser_fail {"status": "success", "data": { "incomplete": "json" Test parser resilience and graceful failure when receiving malformed JSON.

docs.title: Persona Simulation
docs.text:
These scenarios help test how your application handles different tones and complexity levels.

Scenario ID Suggested Keywords Example Response Template Testing Goal persona_grumpy grumpy, rude Ugh, again? Fine. The answer is 42. I hope you're happy now that you've wasted my time. Test tone/sentiment analysis and user experience with rude responses. persona_technical technical, jargon The architecture leverages a decoupled asynchronous event-driven micro-kernel to ensure idempotent state transitions across the distributed ledger. Test readability, accessibility, and summarization capabilities.
